{{Short description|Cutting a square from a rectangle}}
{{for|a term of [[technical drawing]]|Rabattement (drafting)}}
[[File:Rabatment rectangle.png|thumb|The dotted line represents one of two possible rabatments of the rectangle]]

'''Rabatment of the rectangle''' is a compositional technique used as an aid for the placement of objects or the division of space within a rectangular frame, or as an aid for the study of art.

Every rectangle contains two implied squares, each consisting of a short side of the rectangle, an equal length along each longer side, and an imaginary fourth line parallel to the short side. The process of mentally rotating the short sides onto the long ones is called "rabatment", and often the imaginary fourth line is called "the rabatment".

==Theory==
There is no absolute explanation of the mechanism of this method, but there are various theories.<ref name=Mize2009/> One argument is that squares are such a simple, primal geometric shape that the brain automatically looks for them, mentally completing this rabatment whether it is made explicit or not. When a composition uses elements of the scene to match, the square feels complete in itself, producing a feeling of harmony.<ref name=Mize2009/>

==Practice==
[[File:Rabatment animation.gif|thumb|Animation of a rabatment line within a rectangle]]
[[Renaissance]] artists used rabatment as a foundation to art and architectural works,<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZZjk2PCBrj8C&pg=PA122 |page=122 |first1=Bharath |last1=Sriraman |first2=Viktor |last2=Freiman |first3=Nicole |last3=Lirette-Pitre |title=Interdisciplinarity, creativity, and learning: mathematics with literature, paradoxes, history, technology, and modeling |publisher=IAP |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-60752-101-3}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |url=http://www.math.umt.edu/TMME/vol3no2/TMMEvol3no2_Montana_pp157_175.pdf |last=Fett |first=Birch |title=An In-depth Investigation of the Divine Ratio |publisher=The Montana Council of Teachers of Mathematics |year=2006 |journal=The Montana Mathematics Enthusiast |issn=1551-3440 |volume=3 |number=2 |pages=157–175 |doi=10.54870/1551-3440.1047 |archive-date=2015-03-22 |access-date=2011-02-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150322042427/http://www.math.umt.edu/tmme/vol3no2/TMMEvol3no2_Montana_pp157_175.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> but the rabatment can be observed in art taken from almost any period.<ref>{{cite book |title=The painter's secret geometry: a study of composition in art |last=Bouleau |first=Charles |pages=43–46 |publisher=Harcourt, Brace |year=1963 |location=New York }}</ref>

As one of many composition techniques, rabatment of the rectangle can be used to inform the positioning of elements within the rectangle. There is no hard and fast rule regarding such positioning; a composition can have a sense of dynamic unrest or a sense of equilibrium relative to important lines such as ones taken from rabatment or from the rule of thirds, or from nodal points such as the "eyes of a rectangle"—the four intersections derived from the rule of thirds.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.giotto.us/vasari/feltus/composition.html |last=Feltus |first=Alan |title=Painting and Composition |publisher=International School of Painting, Drawing, and Sculpture |location=Umbria, Italy |access-date=26 February 2011 |archive-date=9 October 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111009031831/http://www.giotto.us/vasari/feltus/composition.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> Primary image elements can be positioned within one of the two rabatment squares to define the center of interest, and secondary image elements can be placed outside of a rabatment square.<ref name=Mize2008>{{cite web |url=https://visualcomposing.blogspot.com/2008/07/placing-our-images-rabatment.html |title=Placing Our Images: Rabatment |last=Mize |first=Dianne |work=Compose |date=16 July 2008 |access-date=27 February 2011}}</ref>

The concept of rabatment can be applied to rectangles of any proportion.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FnvsAAAAMAAJ |title=Composing your paintings |last=Dunstan |first=Bernard |pages=22, 26 |publisher=Taplinger Publishing |year=1979 |isbn=0-8008-1803-2 |series=Start To Paint}}</ref> For rectangles with a 3:2 ratio (as in [[135 film|35mm film]] in still photography), it happens that the rabatment lines are exactly matched to the [[rule of thirds]] lines.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.watercoloristsofwhatcom.com/glossary.html |title=Glossary |publisher=Watercolorists of Whatcom |last=Brown |first=Scott |year=2009 |access-date=27 February 2011 |archive-date=20 March 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120320202723/http://www.watercoloristsofwhatcom.com/glossary.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In a horizontally-aligned rectangle, there is one implied square for the left side and one for the right; for a vertically-aligned rectangle, there are upper and lower squares.<ref name=Mize2009>{{cite web |url=http://emptyeasel.com/2009/01/27/how-to-use-rabatment-in-your-compositions/ |title=How to Use Rabatment in Your Compositions |last=Mize |first=Dianne |work=Empty Easel |date=27 January 2009 |access-date=26 February 2011}}</ref> If the long sides of the rectangle are exactly twice the length of the short, this line is right in the middle. With longer-proportioned rectangles, the squares don't overlap, but with shorter-proportioned ones, they do. In [[Western culture]]s that read left to right, attention is often focused inside the left-hand rabatment, or on the line it forms at the right-hand side of the image.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.explore-drawing-and-painting.com/composition-art.html |title=Composition in art: Rabatment |publisher=Explore-Drawing-and-Painting.com |last=Nelson |first=Connie |year=2010 |access-date=1 March 2011 |archive-date=10 July 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110710212037/http://www.explore-drawing-and-painting.com/composition-art.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

When rabatment is used with one side of a [[golden rectangle]], and then iteratively applied to the left-over rectangle, the resulting "whirling rectangles" describe the [[golden spiral]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Fairbanks |first1=Avard T. |last2=Fairbanks |first2=Eugene F. |title=Human Proportions for Artists |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=RacMqZ-sCDQC&pg=PA210 210] |publisher=Fairbanks Art and Books |year=2005 |isbn=0-9725841-1-0}}</ref>
